I'm not arguing they don't, that's my favorite cryptography textbook :) from a pedagogical perspective, that split makes a lot of sense. From a library management perspective, I don't think the conversation of "is this public key or secret key" will be a helpful one for more advanced protocols which intermingle aspects of both.

On my end, the split that makes sense is Crypto/{Assumptions,Foundations,Primitives,Protocols,Reductions}.

In Assumptions, you'd put the definition of discrete log hardness, RSA hardness, LWE, and so on.

In Foundations, you'd put things like the random oracle model, negligibility, security games, and so on.

In Primitives you'd put the tools from complexity theory that you end up using, such as PRFs, hash functions, PRGs, and so on.

In Protocols you'd put higher level things built up from those basic primitives, such as MACs, (Public or Private Key) Encryption Schemes, and so on.

Then in Reductions you prove that the security of these schemes, or specific instances of them, reduce to certain assumptions either in a generic (depending on the relation underlying the Sigma Protocol) or specific way (like DLog for Schnorr).

This isn't quite what I did on my fork, but its how I'd change things if I were to do it again.

Little late to the party here, but I wanted to comment on some choices we made at VCVio that I feel would be relevant for any similar crypto framework in Cslib:

  1. One choice is to model protocols as directly returning (sub)probability distributions, which seems to be the path taken by the the above PRs on perfect secrecy and sigma protocol. This choice is straightforward, but comes with the following limitations:
  • Your protocols are noncomputable and for (ideal) modeling purposes only
  • You will need to add extensions eventually to things like the random oracle model, necessitating an oracle query framework (which, I argue below, is the right starting point for modeling protocols, delaying the conversion to (sub-)PMFs)
  • It is hard to "inspect" into the protocol or computation; for instance, a rewinding extractor for Schnorr's signature (going from special soundness => unforgeability) will need to stop the adversary at some random oracle query, preserve its randomness, then answer with a different response. It can be done (https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/573.pdf) but with lots of stateful reasoning
  1. Because of the above, a better option is to model your computation as a free monad or (inductive) interaction tree.

This way, your computations are maximally uninterpreted, you can model probability as querying from a random sampling oracle, you can add random oracles as an easy extension, and later on you can substitute all these calls to either: (i) return uniformly (for ideal protocol modeling & proof), or (ii) return using a concrete PRG or hash function (leading to executable protocols matching with, say, FIPS spec).

There are also all kinds of ways you can interpret your computation: by composing handlers, you can easily add tracking, counting, or caching capabilities into your oracle implementation.

There's also some nuance with which free monad construction should be used. The current definition in Cslib is over an arbitrary type constructor:

inductive FreeM.{u, v, w} (F : Type u → Type v) (α : Type w) where

While maximally general, this also bumps the universe of the type, which disallows us from putting free monads inside themselves (which would happen when you model interactive protocols using continuations, with each step being an oracle computation).

In contrast, if you restrict to free monad over a polynomial functor, then it's still general enough for all crypto situations I can think of, and you avoid the universe bump:

inductive FreeM' (A : Type uA) (B: A → Type uB) : Type v → Type (max uA uB v)

A special case of the above is when you specialize the response type to be uniform instead of dependent on the query type. This "single oracle" case doesn't seem to nicely model protocols with multiple oracles, and we can get full dependency without paying any cost.

  1. An even further point for inter-operability is to have a general type class for "monadic computations that can denote into (sub-)probability distributions". This way all results can be stated relative to such type classes, and we can swap between monads - for instance, my monad in VCVio may be different from the monad in Cslib, or in yet another library (for example Aeneas or Hax or Bas' upcoming library).

  2. There are further features in VCVio that I would argue should be present in any verified crypto framework:

  • a probabilistic program logic, ideally done in a manner compatible with monad transformer stack on top of original computation type (state + error), with good tactic support (mvcgen-style but generalized)
  • cost abstraction & accounting, allowing us to state the efficiency of adversaries and reductions, and precisely quantify them in a given proof

We are now in the (fortunate) situation that verified code is cheap! But that also means we should set up the infrastructure to make sure that formalization can scale, and that our formalization doesn't just capture idealized protocols in papers & textbooks but can bridge the gap to actual, messy implementations (this has been done before in other frameworks e.g. Easycrypt)

We can certainly define generic definitions to be monad-agnostic. For instance, this is what is in VCVio right now:

/-- An `AsymmEncAlg` with message space `M`, key spaces `PK` and `SK`, and ciphertexts in `C`.
`m` is the monad used to execute key generation, encryption, and decryption. The scheme data stays
purely algorithmic; probabilistic semantics and public-randomness injection are supplied
separately when defining security experiments. -/
@[ext]
structure AsymmEncAlg (m : Type → Type u) [Monad m] (M PK SK C : Type) where
  keygen : m (PK × SK)
  encrypt : (pk : PK) → (msg : M) →  m C
  decrypt : (sk : SK) → (c : C) →  m (Option M)

/-- An explicit-coins asymmetric encryption scheme in the monad `m`.

Key generation runs in `m`, while encryption and decryption become pure once the randomness type
`R` is supplied explicitly. This is the natural refinement used by FO-style transforms, where the
coins are sampled externally or derived from an oracle. -/
structure AsymmEncAlg.ExplicitCoins (m : Type → Type u) [Monad m] (M PK SK R C : Type) where
  keygen : m (PK × SK)

import Mathlib

def barrettMod3319 (a : UInt32) : UInt32 :=
  let m    : UInt64 := 1294054
  let q    : UInt64 := (a.toUInt64 * m) >>> 32
  let r    : UInt32 := a - q.toUInt32 * 3319
  let t    : UInt32 := r - 3319
  let mask : UInt32 := (0 : UInt32) - (t >>> 31)
  t + (mask &&& 3319)

attribute [grind =] UInt64.toNat_ofNat' UInt64.toNat_mul UInt64.toNat_shiftRight
attribute [grind =] UInt32.toNat_ofNat' UInt32.ofNat_sub UInt32.ofNat_mul UInt32.ofNat_uInt64ToNat
  UInt32.toNat_shiftRight UInt32.toNat_sub UInt32.zero_and UInt32.toNat_zero UInt32.ofNat_toNat
  UInt32.ofNat_mod UInt32.toUInt64_ofNat'
attribute [grind =] Nat.shiftRight_eq_div_pow

lemma barrettMod3319aux (a : ℕ) (ha : a < UInt32.size) :
    (barrettMod3319 (.ofNat a)).toNat = a % 3319 := by
  -- unwrap the definition of the function
  have h₁ : (UInt32.ofNat a).toUInt64 = UInt64.ofNat a := by grind
  rw [barrettMod3319, h₁]
  -- re-introduce the variables so it's readable
  set m : UInt64 := 1294054
  set q : UInt64 := (.ofNat a * m) >>> 32
  set r : UInt32 := .ofNat a - q.toUInt32 * 3319
  set t : UInt32 := r - 3319
  set mask : UInt32 := (0 : UInt32) - t >>> 31
  -- computation of `q` doesn't overflow
  set Q : ℕ := (a * 1294054) >>> 32
  have hq : q.toNat = Q := by grind
  -- computation of R doesn't underflow, also it's small
  set R : ℕ := a - Q * 3319
  obtain ⟨hr, hR⟩ : r.toNat = R ∧ R < 5389 := by
    have : .ofNat R = r := by grind
    grind
  -- computation of T can overflow but not much
  set T : ℕ := (2 ^ 32 - 3319 + R) % 2 ^ 32
  have ht : t.toNat = T := by grind
  -- in both cases, the mask is correct and we get the right answer
  obtain hR' | hR' : 3319 ≤ R ∨ R < 3319 := by grind
  · -- have hT : T = R - 3319 := by grind
    suffices t >>> 31 = 0 by grind
    apply UInt32.toNat.inj
    grind
  · suffices t >>> 31 = 1 by grind
    apply UInt32.toNat.inj
    grind


lemma barrettMod3319_correct (a : UInt32) :
    barrettMod3319 a = a % 3319 := by calc
  barrettMod3319 a = .ofNat (barrettMod3319 (.ofNat a.toNat)).toNat := by grind
  _ = a % 3319 := by grind [barrettMod3319aux]
